# Pandora Papers Reporting Concerning King Abdullah II of Jordan  
**Report date: October 1, 2026**

## List of Queries and Tool Calls Made

1. A Tavily search was conducted for:  
   **“Pandora Papers King Abdullah II Jordan offshore property network shell companies properties addresses ICIJ investigation”**  
   The search returned four benchmark sources: **SRC-001, SRC-002, SRC-003, and SRC-004**.

2. A research reflection noted that the first search found broad figures, locations, British Virgin Islands incorporation, three Malibu companies, and responses, but did not provide a comprehensive entity-by-entity inventory, exact addresses, intermediaries, transaction chronology, or source-grounded registry details.

3. A second Tavily search was conducted for:  
   **“site:icij.org/investigations/pandora-papers/jordan-king-abdullah-luxury-property companies Malibu Ascot names Trident Trust Amicorp”** and  
   **“King Abdullah Pandora Papers company names Malibu Washington Ascot London BVI addresses Guardian”**  
   The search returned the same four benchmark sources and added no company names, intermediary names, or exact addresses.

4. A second research reflection concluded that the available retrieved evidence supports only a careful high-level inventory and that exact company names, intermediaries, financing, or precise street addresses should not be claimed when absent from the excerpts.

---

## Fully Comprehensive Findings

### 1. Nature and scope of the reporting

The Pandora Papers investigation was described as a global investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and a team of approximately 150 news outlets, including DW’s Turkish service. It was based on leaked offshore data. [SRC-001]

The Al Jazeera report described the Pandora Papers probe as involving approximately 600 journalists and being based on a leak of approximately 11.9 million documents from 14 global financial services companies. [SRC-003]

The Guardian described the Pandora Papers as “the largest ever trove of leaked offshore data.” It stated that the trove consisted of 11.9 million files leaked from 14 offshore service providers, totaling 2.94 terabytes, and that the files were larger in volume than both the Panama Papers and Paradise Papers. [SRC-002]

The Guardian stated that the files were leaked to ICIJ, which shared access with the Guardian, the BBC, and other media outlets around the world. The ICIJ, described as a Washington, DC-based journalism nonprofit, did not identify the source of the leaked documents. It gave remote access to journalists in 117 countries, including reporters at the Washington Post, Le Monde, El País, Süddeutsche Zeitung, PBS Frontline, and the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. In the United Kingdom, the investigation was led by the Guardian and BBC Panorama. [SRC-002]

The Al Jazeera report stated that the records dated back to the 1970s, although most of the files covered the period from 1996 to 2020. It stated that the documents came from financial services companies in jurisdictions including the British Virgin Islands, Panama, Belize, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, and Switzerland, and that the service providers operated in 38 jurisdictions. [SRC-003]

### 2. Core allegation concerning King Abdullah II

The Guardian reported that King Abdullah II had spent the preceding decades amassing an international luxury property empire “worth well in excess of $100m (£74m),” with a footprint stretching “from the clifftops of Malibu, California, to Washington DC and on to central London’s most exclusive postcodes.” [SRC-002]

The report stated that Abdullah had built the property empire “showing the same zeal for secrecy he has demonstrated when asked about his finances at home.” It alleged that he had disguised his ownership through a series of offshore companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, according to records shared by ICIJ with the Guardian, the BBC, and other media outlets around the world. [SRC-002]

The Al Jazeera report stated that the documents showed how King Abdullah II created “a network of offshore companies and tax havens” to amass a $100 million property empire extending from Malibu, California, to Washington, DC, and London. [SRC-003]

DW reported that the monarch had used money from various offshore accounts to buy properties between 2003 and 2017. It stated that he was said to have purchased 14 houses and flats in the United States and the United Kingdom for a total of more than €91 million ($106 million), through 36 front companies registered in tax havens. [SRC-001]

According to DW, trust-firm sources quoted in the reporting generally referred to King Abdullah as the “final beneficiary” living in Jordan, or as “You know who” from Jordan. [SRC-001]

The reporting characterizes the use of offshore companies and the concealment of ownership as journalistic findings or allegations based on leaked records. The retrieved excerpts do not provide the names of the 36 companies, the names of the offshore accounts, or a complete company-by-company ownership chain. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

### 3. Shell companies and other entities

#### Directly identified entities

The retrieved sources identify the following categories of entities:

- **36 front companies registered in tax havens**, according to DW. [SRC-001]
- **A series of offshore companies incorporated in the British Virgin Islands**, according to the Guardian. [SRC-002]
- **Three offshore companies used to purchase three Malibu beachfront mansions**, according to the Al Jazeera report. [SRC-003]
- **The Royal Hashemite Court**, which issued a statement concerning the properties. [SRC-001; SRC-003; SRC-004]
- **DLA Piper**, identified as the law firm representing the monarch. [SRC-003; SRC-004]
- **The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists**, which shared the leaked records with participating media organizations. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

No exact names of the 36 front companies or of the three offshore companies used for the Malibu purchases appear in the retrieved excerpts. No trust names, account names, holding-company names, banks, corporate service providers, directors, shareholders, or registration numbers appear in the retrieved excerpts. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

#### General offshore-company context

The Guardian explained that offshore service providers offer corporate services to individuals or companies seeking to do business offshore. Their clients typically seek to discreetly set up companies or trusts in lightly regulated tax havens such as the British Virgin Islands, Panama, the Cook Islands, and the U.S. state of South Dakota. Companies registered offshore can hold assets such as property, aircraft, yachts, and investments in stocks and shares. Holding assets in an offshore company can hide from the public the identity of the person to whom the assets actually belong, or the “beneficial owner.” [SRC-002]

The Guardian stated that offshore jurisdictions tend to have no income or corporation taxes and can be attractive to wealthy individuals and companies that do not want to pay taxes in their home countries. It also stated that offshore jurisdictions tend to be highly secretive and publish little or no information about companies or trusts incorporated there. [SRC-002]

The Guardian emphasized that moving money offshore is not in itself illegal and that there can be legitimate reasons to do so. It stated that not everyone named in the Pandora Papers is suspected of wrongdoing. [SRC-002]

The Al Jazeera report stated that, in most countries, it is not illegal to have assets offshore or to use shell companies to do business across national borders. [SRC-003]

### 4. Beneficial ownership, ownership, management, control, and nominee relationships

DW stated that trust-firm sources referred to King Abdullah as the “final beneficiary” living in Jordan, or as “You know who” from Jordan. [SRC-001]

The Guardian alleged that Abdullah had disguised his ownership of the properties through a series of BVI-incorporated offshore companies. [SRC-002]

The Al Jazeera report stated that the three Malibu mansions were purchased through three offshore companies “by the King of Jordan.” [SRC-003]

The retrieved excerpts do not identify the directors, officers, shareholders, trustees, protectors, nominees, agents, advisers, or corporate-service intermediaries connected with any of the companies. They also do not provide a documented chain showing how King Abdullah allegedly controlled or managed each entity. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

The retrieved excerpts do not establish whether the king was the registered legal owner of any property, whether he was a shareholder or director of any company, whether a nominee held shares or title on his behalf, or whether any trust existed in the ownership structure. The available reporting uses the terms “final beneficiary,” “front companies,” “offshore companies,” and “disguised his ownership,” but does not provide the underlying registry entries or full leaked-document extracts in the retrieved material. [SRC-001; SRC-002]

### 5. Intermediaries, lawyers, advisers, nominees, agents, journalists, and organizations

#### Lawyers and law firm

DLA Piper was identified as the law firm representing King Abdullah. The firm stated:

> “Any implication that there is something improper about ownership of property through companies in offshore jurisdictions is categorically denied.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The firm also stated:

> “[Abdullah] has not at any point misused public monies or made any use whatsoever of the proceeds of aid or assistance intended for public use.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The retrieved excerpts do not identify any individual lawyer at DLA Piper. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

#### Royal Hashemite Court

The Royal Hashemite Court issued a statement confirming that the monarch owned properties abroad for diplomatic visits and consultations. It said that, for security reasons, it had been important to keep details of the properties secret. It also stated that none of the purchases had been funded by the state treasury or by foreign grants or loans that Jordan had received as foreign assistance. [SRC-001]

The Al Jazeera report quoted the royal palace as saying that the properties in the United States and United Kingdom were “no secret” and that privacy and security reasons explained why they had not been disclosed. The palace statement said:

> “This is not unusual nor improper.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

It also stated:

> “The cost of these properties and all related expenditures have been personally funded by His Majesty. None of these expenses have been funded by the state budget or treasury.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The palace stated that the properties were used during official visits and that some were used during private visits. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

#### Journalists and organizations

The reporting involved ICIJ, the Guardian, the BBC, BBC Panorama, DW, Al Jazeera, and other media organizations. The Guardian stated that the investigation provided remote access to journalists in 117 countries. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

The retrieved excerpts do not identify any offshore corporate intermediary, trust company, accountant, banker, nominee, agent, adviser, or property broker involved in King Abdullah’s alleged network. The search reflection specifically noted that searches for names including Trident Trust and Amicorp did not produce additional benchmark evidence. No such names should therefore be treated as part of the reported network based on the retrieved sources. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003; SRC-004]

### 6. Jurisdictions and corporate-registration locations

The Guardian specifically identified the **British Virgin Islands (BVI)** as the place where the offshore companies used to disguise ownership were incorporated. [SRC-002]

DW described the 36 front companies as registered in “tax havens.” It did not identify the jurisdictions of each company in the retrieved excerpt. [SRC-001]

The Al Jazeera report stated generally that more than two-thirds of the nearly 1,000 companies identified by ICIJ in the broader Pandora Papers investigation were set up in the British Virgin Islands. This statistic concerns the broader investigation and does not establish that more than two-thirds of King Abdullah’s companies were BVI companies. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The broader Pandora Papers records were drawn from financial-services companies in the British Virgin Islands, Panama, Belize, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, and Switzerland. The retrieved sources do not state that King Abdullah had companies registered in each of those jurisdictions. [SRC-003]

The Guardian’s general explanation also identifies Panama, the Cook Islands, and the U.S. state of South Dakota as examples of lightly regulated or secretive offshore jurisdictions used by clients of offshore service providers, but the retrieved excerpts do not connect those jurisdictions specifically to King Abdullah’s alleged property network. [SRC-002]

### 7. Properties and luxury-real-estate locations

#### Malibu, California

The reporting identified three beachfront or clifftop mansions on California’s Malibu coast. [SRC-002; SRC-003]

The Al Jazeera report stated:

> “Three beachfront mansions in Malibu [were] purchased through three offshore companies for $68 million by the King of Jordan in the years after Jordanians filled the streets during Arab Spring to protest joblessness and corruption.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The Guardian described one of the Malibu properties as perhaps the most palatial and certainly the most expensive of the king’s purchases revealed in the Pandora Papers. It described the property as a vast clifftop estate containing a “resort hotel-like mega mansion” with 26 rooms. The property overlooked a stretch of coastline made famous as the location of the dramatic final scene in the original 1968 *Planet of the Apes* film. [SRC-002]

The Guardian stated that Abdullah acquired three clifftop properties on California’s Malibu coast. [SRC-002]

No street address, parcel number, neighborhood beyond Malibu, seller, purchaser entity name, closing date, financing information, or title-record reference appears in the retrieved excerpts. [SRC-002; SRC-003]

#### Washington, DC

The Al Jazeera report stated that Abdullah owned three luxury apartments in a Washington, DC, complex with panoramic views of the Potomac River. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

No building name, street address, neighborhood, apartment numbers, purchase dates, purchase prices, financing arrangements, or company names appear in the retrieved excerpts. [SRC-003]

#### Ascot, England

The Al Jazeera report stated that Abdullah owned a house in Ascot, described as one of England’s most expensive towns. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

No street address, neighborhood, purchase date, purchase price, financing information, or company name appears in the retrieved excerpts. [SRC-003]

#### Central London

The Guardian stated that the property empire extended to central London’s most exclusive postcodes. [SRC-002]

The Al Jazeera report stated that Abdullah owned multimillion-dollar apartments in central London. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

No exact London address, postcode, neighborhood name, building name, apartment number, purchase date, purchase price, financing arrangement, or ownership-company name appears in the retrieved excerpts. [SRC-002; SRC-003]

#### United States and United Kingdom generally

DW stated that 14 houses and flats in the United States and United Kingdom were purchased between 2003 and 2017 for more than €91 million ($106 million). [SRC-001]

The royal statements confirmed ownership of properties abroad in the United States and United Kingdom and said they were used for diplomatic visits, consultations, official visits, and, in some cases, private visits. [SRC-001; SRC-003]

The retrieved excerpts do not reconcile the reported total of 14 houses and flats with the separately described three Malibu mansions, three Washington apartments, one Ascot house, and the multimillion-dollar central London apartments. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

### 8. Purchases, transfers, sales, financing, and other transactions

DW reported that the properties were purchased between 2003 and 2017. [SRC-001]

The Al Jazeera report stated that the three Malibu mansions were purchased for $68 million in the years after the Arab Spring protests. [SRC-003]

The Guardian stated that the properties were acquired during a period when U.S. economic and military aid to Jordan quadrupled and Jordanian citizens were subjected to austerity as part of an International Monetary Fund bailout for the resource-poor country. This is contextual reporting and does not itself establish that aid money financed the properties. [SRC-002]

The Royal Hashemite Court stated that the cost of the properties and all related expenditures were personally funded by King Abdullah and that none of the expenses were funded by the state budget or treasury. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The royal court also stated that none of the purchases were funded by the state treasury or by foreign grants or loans received by Jordan as foreign assistance. [SRC-001]

King Abdullah’s lawyers stated that the properties were bought with personal wealth. They also said that it was common practice for high-profile individuals to buy properties through offshore companies for privacy and security reasons. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The retrieved sources do not identify any sale, transfer, mortgage, loan, refinancing, pledge, lease, construction financing, bank, lender, payment account, or other financing transaction involving the properties. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

The retrieved sources also do not provide documentary evidence in the excerpts establishing the source of the alleged personal wealth used for the purchases. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

### 9. Denials, explanations, and responses

King Abdullah’s lawyers issued an immediate statement rejecting the claim that he had used money that was not his own. The statement said:

> “HM [His Majesty] has not at any point misused public monies or made any use whatsoever of the proceeds of aid or assistance intended for public use … HM cares deeply for Jordan and its people and acts with integrity and in the best interests of his country and its citizens at all times.” [SRC-001]

The Royal Hashemite Court confirmed that the monarch owned properties abroad for diplomatic visits and consultations. It said that the details had been kept secret for security reasons and that none of the purchases were funded by the state treasury or by foreign grants or loans that Jordan had received as foreign assistance. [SRC-001]

The royal palace stated that the properties were “no secret,” that privacy and security explained the lack of disclosure, and that:

> “This is not unusual nor improper.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

The palace further stated:

> “The cost of these properties and all related expenditures have been personally funded by His Majesty. None of these expenses have been funded by the state budget or treasury.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

It said that the properties were used during official visits and that some were used during private visits. [SRC-003; SRC-004]

DLA Piper, identified as the law firm representing the monarch, stated:

> “Any implication that there is something improper about ownership of property through companies in offshore jurisdictions is categorically denied.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

DLA Piper also stated:

> “[Abdullah] has not at any point misused public monies or made any use whatsoever of the proceeds of aid or assistance intended for public use.” [SRC-003; SRC-004]

DW reported that the purchases might have been legal, even though they were disguised, as claimed by the Royal Hashemite Court. [SRC-001]

The Guardian stated that using offshore companies to acquire property is not illegal and is sometimes done to protect privacy or security. It also stated that the secrecy provided by the offshore system can open the door to money laundering, but the retrieved excerpt does not report a finding that King Abdullah committed money laundering. [SRC-002]

### 10. Context concerning Jordan, foreign aid, and public reaction

The Guardian reported that Jordan was propped up by billions of dollars in international financial aid and that unemployment had nearly doubled over the preceding seven years. It described the subject of how much land the king owned as too sensitive for the Jordanian public to know about. [SRC-002]

The Guardian reported that Jordanian lawyer Moayyad al-Majali was detained in October 2019, had his laptop and phones confiscated, and was accused of slandering the country’s ruler after asking: “how much land does the king own?” [SRC-002]

The Guardian stated that the properties were acquired as U.S. economic and military aid to Jordan quadrupled and as Jordanian citizens faced austerity under an IMF bailout for the resource-poor country. [SRC-002]

DW stated that Jordan was one of the poorest countries in the region, lacked the rich oil and gas deposits of many of its neighbors, suffered from water shortages, and had a population of approximately 10 million. It reported that the country had received billions of dollars in development aid from the United States, the European Union, Germany, and other nations. It stated that U.S. aid in 2020 was $1.5 billion/€1.29 billion. [SRC-001]

DW reported that, according to the Jordanian Bureau of Statistics, 25% of the population over age 18 was out of work in the first quarter of the year, while youth unemployment was estimated at approximately 40%. [SRC-001]

DW quoted Karim Merhej, a non-resident fellow at the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, as saying:

> “There is significant discontent toward the monarch, and these revelations are vindicating what a lot of people feel about the monarch. The question is now whether this will lead to any significant political changes in the country.” [SRC-001]

DW reported that, according to the Arab Barometer, in 2018 only 38% of Jordanians said they had some or great trust in the government, while 68% said they had no trust in parliament. It also stated that surveying citizens’ views toward the king or royal family was not allowed. [SRC-001]

DW quoted Dr. Maria Josua, a Middle East analyst at the Hamburg-based research institute GIGA, as saying:

> “I wouldn’t say that the papers have revealed anything sensationally surprising. It has always been clear that the royal family is wealthy and owns properties abroad.” [SRC-001]

Josua also stated:

> “But there have never been direct accusations against the king himself.” [SRC-001]

DW reported that Josua described repression in Jordan as “extremely strong,” stating that unions and professional associations advocating improvements had been closed down or strongly censured. It also reported that a news blackout had been imposed and that the ICIJ website was taken down in Jordan only hours before the Pandora Papers were published on the organization’s website. Josua described this as “the royal attempt to control the narrative.” [SRC-001]

DW reported that revelations would likely contribute to further discontent toward Jordan’s political system, even though the disguised real-estate purchases might have been legal, as claimed by the Royal Hashemite Court. [SRC-001]

The Guardian reported that Moayyad al-Majali’s detention occurred in a country where the subject of the king’s land ownership was considered too sensitive for the public to know about. [SRC-002]

### 11. Foreign-aid explanations and statements

DW stated that, according to current knowledge, development aid had not been funneled to the palace. [SRC-001]

Karim Merhej told DW:

> “Jordan ranks very high on the Open Budget Survey and the Jordanian government has effectively made its finances quite transparent — this is not very surprising given the fact that the country is heavily reliant on grants and loans from other countries and international organizations.” [SRC-001]

DW reported that Germany, which had sent millions in aid to Jordan, appeared fairly sure that the money had gone to intended projects, including assistance for tens of thousands of Syrian refugees. A spokesperson for Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development said:

> “Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) has no knowledge that development cooperation funds for Jordan for which the BMZ is responsible have been made available to the Jordanian royal family. Rather, the structure of our development cooperation with Jordan and the disbursement of corresponding funds is linked to the agreed progress of the respective joint projects.” [SRC-001]

The retrieved sources do not provide an independent audit, bank record, registry record, or other documentary proof in the excerpts either confirming or disproving the stated source of the funds. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

### 12. Journalistic assessments and unresolved uncertainty

The Guardian stated that offshore property acquisition is not illegal and may be done for privacy or security, while also stating that offshore secrecy can open the door to money laundering. [SRC-002]

DW characterized the purchases as “probably not illegal” but said they were at odds with the government’s declared principles of financial transparency. [SRC-001]

Al Jazeera presented the reporting as showing that King Abdullah II had “hidden millions of dollars in offshore tax havens and secretly bought luxury homes,” while also reporting the palace and lawyers’ denials and explanations. [SRC-003]

The sources do not establish, in the retrieved excerpts, that King Abdullah committed tax evasion, money laundering, corruption, misuse of public funds, or any other criminal offense. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

The sources do establish that the reporting alleged offshore ownership structures, offshore-company purchases, and secrecy concerning the properties, while the royal palace and DLA Piper denied impropriety and denied use of public funds or aid. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

### 13. Missing, ambiguous, or contradictory evidence

- The excerpts do not list the names of the 36 front companies. [SRC-001]
- The excerpts do not name the three offshore companies used to acquire the Malibu properties. [SRC-003]
- The excerpts do not provide corporate-registration numbers, registry extracts, incorporation dates, directors, officers, shareholders, trustees, nominees, or agents. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]
- The excerpts do not identify the offshore accounts or trust structures allegedly used. [SRC-001]
- The excerpts do not provide exact street addresses, parcel numbers, building names, apartment numbers, postcodes, or title records for the properties. [SRC-002; SRC-003]
- The excerpts do not identify sellers, brokers, lenders, banks, lawyers other than DLA Piper, accountants, trust companies, or other intermediaries. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]
- The excerpts do not document any sales, transfers, mortgages, loans, refinancing, or other financing arrangements. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]
- The total of 14 houses and flats reported by DW is not reconciled in the excerpts with the separately described three Malibu mansions, three Washington apartments, one Ascot house, and central London apartments. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]
- The reported value is expressed as “more than €91 million ($106 million)” by DW, “well in excess of $100m (£74m)” by the Guardian, and approximately $100 million by Al Jazeera. The excerpts do not explain whether these figures use the same properties, dates, valuations, or exchange rates. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]
- The Guardian states that the properties were acquired as U.S. aid to Jordan quadrupled and austerity occurred, but this is contextual timing and does not establish that U.S. aid financed the properties. [SRC-002]
- The Al Jazeera report describes the three Malibu purchases as occurring “in the years after Jordanians filled the streets during Arab Spring,” while DW gives the broader purchase period as 2003–2017. The excerpts do not give exact purchase dates for the Malibu properties. [SRC-001; SRC-003]
- The royal palace says that the properties were “no secret,” while the reporting states that ownership was disguised through offshore companies and that the details had been kept secret for privacy and security. These statements concern different aspects of disclosure and are not fully reconciled in the excerpts. [SRC-002; SRC-003]
- SRC-004 has an ICIJ URL and the title **“While foreign aid poured in, Jordan's King Abdullah funnelled $100 million into luxury homes,”** but the retrieved excerpt is textually the same as the Al Jazeera report and displays the Al Jazeera headline and page material. This source-label/content mismatch is preserved rather than resolved. [SRC-004]
- The source excerpts identify DLA Piper as representing the monarch but do not identify any individual lawyer. [SRC-003; SRC-004]
- The retrieved material does not show the underlying leaked documents or registry records themselves; it reports descriptions of those materials. [SRC-001; SRC-002; SRC-003]

---

## List of All Relevant Sources (with citations in the report)

### [SRC-001] Pandora Papers: The royal “you know who” from Jordan  
DW, Jennifer Holleis, October 4, 2021  
https://www.dw.com/en/pandora-papers-the-king-of-jordans-hidden-property-gems/a-59403014

Used for: the reported 2003–2017 purchase period; 14 U.S. and U.K. houses and flats; total exceeding €91 million/$106 million; 36 front companies registered in tax havens; “final beneficiary” and “You know who” wording; royal and lawyers’ responses; statements concerning diplomatic use, secrecy, foreign aid, Jordanian finances, public reaction, and the ICIJ website being taken down in Jordan.

### [SRC-002] King of Jordan hidden property empire worth more than $100m, Pandora papers reveal  
The Guardian, Simon Goodley and Michael Safi, October 3, 2021  
https://www.theguardian.com/news/2021/oct/03/king-of-jordan-hidden-property-empire-worth-more-than-100m-pandora-papers-reveal

Used for: the alleged property empire exceeding $100 million; BVI incorporation; Malibu, Washington, and central London locations; the 26-room Malibu “resort hotel-like mega mansion”; contextual reporting concerning aid, austerity, IMF support, offshore structures, the scope and origin of the Pandora Papers, and the explanation that offshore ownership is not inherently illegal.

### [SRC-003] Investigation reveals offshore assets of heads of state  
Al Jazeera, October 3, 2021, updated October 4, 2021  
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/10/3/investigation-reveals-offshore-assets-of-heads-of-state

Used for: the three Malibu mansions and $68 million figure; three Washington, DC, apartments; Ascot house; central London apartments; the three offshore companies; palace and DLA Piper responses; broader Pandora Papers scope, jurisdictions, dates, and the statement that more than two-thirds of the broader set of companies were established in the BVI.

ICIJ URL as returned by the benchmark tool; retrieved excerpt duplicates the Al Jazeera text and displays Al Jazeera page content
